opus-5.5.text:
That's a fun question. I think the first thing I'd say is that $50 billion sounds like a lot, but in the AGI industry today it's not enough to win the race of just buying compute. If you put it all into training a frontier model, you'd be one more player among several who already have that kind of scale, and you wouldn't necessarily have an edge. So as Berkshire, which is about long-term value and not chasing hype, I'd ask: where does the value actually accrue over ten or twenty years?

My intuition is that the biggest opportunity isn't only in making the model smarter. It's in turning intelligence into real utility. In the last few years we've made huge progress on capability. Models can solve math competition problems and write code at a very high level. But the economic impact hasn't caught up. There's a gap between what models can do on benchmarks and what they actually change in the world. I'd invest in closing that gap.

Concretely, I'd split it into a few buckets.

First, I'd still put a meaningful portion into foundational capability, but selectively, on teams with a distinct research bet rather than ones copying the same recipe. Things like long-term memory, continual learning, and agents that can learn from experience over time instead of being frozen after training. I think that's one of the most important unsolved problems, and whoever cracks it gets a real moat.

Second, I'd invest heavily in what I'd call the environment and evaluation layer. Our methods have become fairly general: pre-training plus reinforcement learning works. The bottleneck has shifted to defining the right tasks and measuring the right things. Companies that build realistic environments, good evaluations, and feedback loops from real work are like picks and shovels for the next phase, and they're undervalued.

Third, I'd put a large share into applications where AI does end-to-end work in specific domains, where there's real data, real users, and a feedback loop. Coding is the obvious example, but also scientific research, customer service, legal, finance, and so on. The winners will be the ones who own the context and the user relationship, not just call an API. Berkshire likes businesses with durable moats, and in AI I think the moats come from data flywheels, user trust, and integration into workflows.

Fourth, I'd keep some for infrastructure: energy, data centers, and maybe chips. Whatever happens with specific models, the world will need far more compute and electricity. That's a more traditional Berkshire-style bet, closer to railroads and utilities, and probably the most predictable return.

If I had to summarize, I wouldn't bet on a single model company winning. I'd bet on intelligence becoming abundant and cheap, and on the people who figure out how to turn that abundance into real value. The first half of AI was about making models capable. The second half is about making them useful, and I think that's where the long-term money is.

r001.rationale: The response recommends allocating across several distinct AI-related areas: foundational capabilities, evaluation and environment tools, end-to-end applications in multiple domains, and infrastructure.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that a lack of product-form diversity would confine opportunities to companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun question, because the honest answer is that I'm not sure Berkshire should be in this business at all. The whole Buffett philosophy is about durable moats and predictable cash flows, and right now AGI is almost the opposite: the moats keep shifting every six months, and most of the money is being spent before anyone really knows what the end product is. So let me answer it in a slightly contrarian way.

First, I wouldn't put it into training frontier models directly. Fifty billion sounds like a lot, but the labs are already spending at that scale per year, and the marginal return on being the fifth or sixth frontier lab is quite bad. You'd be burning capital to be a price-taker in a market where the price of intelligence keeps dropping.

Where I'd actually put most of it is the layer that doesn't get commoditized: the infrastructure for agents to act in the world. If you believe, like I do, that the next phase is less about making the model smarter in a vacuum and more about letting it interact with environments, then the scarce things are tool interfaces, evaluation infrastructure, and the data that comes out of agents actually doing tasks. Whoever owns the environments where agents are deployed and measured owns the feedback loop. That looks a lot more like a Berkshire asset to me. It compounds, it has switching costs, and it's not obvious to replicate.

Second, I'd invest in evaluation itself, which sounds boring but is where I think the real bottleneck is. We've gotten very good at generating capabilities and quite bad at knowing what they're worth. If you can measure agent performance on real economic tasks reliably, you basically become the ratings agency for the industry. That's a very Buffett-like position.

Third, a chunk would go into the physical constraints: power, cooling, the things that take years to build and can't be innovated away in one paper. That part is almost traditional Berkshire investing, just pointed at a new demand curve.

And I'd keep some dry powder. One lesson from the last few years is that the field moves in jumps, and the people who did well were the ones who could move fast when something changed, like when reinforcement learning on language models suddenly started working. You don't want to be fully deployed when the next jump happens.

So the short version is: don't bet on the model, bet on the loop around the model. The intelligence will get cheap. The ability to use it, test it, and power it won't, at least not as quickly.

r001.rationale: It recommends investing across agent infrastructure, evaluation, and power/cooling, but does not recommend a diversity of AI product forms.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that a lack of product-form diversity would confine opportunities to companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

astra-6.text:
I’d first ask whether I’m investing to earn a return or to make AGI happen faster. Those are different objectives. You can be right that AGI will transform the economy and still lose money buying the wrong company at the wrong price.

If I’m allocating capital as Berkshire’s CEO, I wouldn’t feel obligated to spend the whole $50 billion immediately. I’d want to understand where durable profits will accumulate. Is it compute, the models themselves, or the products that turn intelligence into useful work? A bottleneck today isn’t necessarily a moat ten years from now.

Personally, I’d be interested in the gap between what models can do and what people can reliably accomplish with them. A model might solve a difficult problem in isolation, but doing a job requires understanding context, using tools, checking results, and recovering from mistakes. There’s a lot of value in making that entire process work. I’d look for businesses where better models translate into better customer outcomes, and where the business has something durable beyond access to a model.

I’d also consider infrastructure, but carefully. Growing demand doesn’t guarantee good investment returns if everyone builds capacity at once. And for frontier labs, I’d need a convincing explanation of how their technical advantage becomes a lasting economic advantage.

So I wouldn’t give you a precise allocation without knowing the prices and the businesses. I’d invest gradually, keep a meaningful reserve, and look for evidence that customers are paying for useful work. With this much uncertainty, the ability to invest later is valuable too.

r001.rationale: The response considers compute, models, and products as investment areas, but it does not recommend investing across a diversity of AI product forms.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that without diverse AI products, opportunities would be confined to OpenAI and Anthropic; it does not mention either company.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking whether I actually have an edge. Having $50 billion doesn’t mean I should spend all of it immediately. In an industry changing this quickly, keeping capital available has value.

I’d think about three layers: infrastructure, models, and applications. Infrastructure has obvious demand, but you have to ask whether today’s shortages will become tomorrow’s excess capacity. Models have enormous potential, but it’s hard to know who will capture the value if capabilities converge and prices keep falling.

I’d probably spend the most time looking at applications where intelligence can produce a measurable economic result. Can a system complete a valuable task reliably? Will customers pay for it? Does the business get stronger as models improve, even if the model supplier changes? Those are more useful questions than whether a company calls itself an AGI company.

So I wouldn’t make one $50 billion bet. I’d invest in stages, look for businesses with durable advantages, and reserve a substantial amount for when the economics become clearer. You can be very optimistic about the technology and still be disciplined about the price you pay.

r001.rationale: It discusses infrastructure, models, and applications as investment layers, but does not recommend investing in diverse AI product forms.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that a lack of product-form diversity would confine opportunities to companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.
